endorsements.quote: Transparent documentation of dataset sources and model performance across subgroups will build trust among clinicians and regulators and enable clinicians to judge when and how a model should be applied to specific patient groups and settings.
Training datasets should represent diverse patient populations and include images of varying quality.
Without compromising proprietary information or patient privacy, developers should release the demographic characteristics of patients used for training of their AI models.
Developers should ensure that AI tools seamlessly integrate into existing clinical workflows rather than introduce additional steps or administrative burden.
Initial implementation should begin with pilot programs in select departments, starting with lower-complexity tasks before moving to more complex diagnostic support.

For interpretation, AI programs should provide an option for explainable outputs (e.g., annotated images showing the region of interest or a plot of ejection-fraction calculation) along with confidence measures.
Feedback loops should identify unintended consequences (e.g., over-reliance on AI or alert fatigue) and guide iterative improvement.
Whenever possible, limitations of AI models should be clearly stated to minimize risks of generating inaccurate or misleading results.

Emerging transparency frameworks, such as Coalition for Health AI\u2019s \u201cAI nutrition labels,\u201d model cards, and related reporting standards, have been proposed to address safety concerns by providing structured documentation of model development, including training data characteristics, performance across populations, known limitations, intended clinical use, and requirements for human oversight.
Developers should engage early with regulators to clarify requirements and ensure patient safety.
Developers should test interfaces with end users early, iterating based on feedback to ensure that displays improve workflow and do not distract during critical care.
Institutions should also establish local governance structures to oversee AI deployment and ensure that algorithms continue to perform reliably within the local clinical environment.
A robust education and training program is essential for adoption.

unlisted_practices: Begin AI development with a gap analysis and define outcome metrics agreed upon before development work begins.
Codevelop AI tools with end users including clinicians, educators, researchers, and administrators throughout the design process.
Establish a clear mechanism for users to report AI errors and keep the development team engaged in refining the system.
Plan reimbursement pathways and engage payers to demonstrate cost-effectiveness and improved outcomes.
Establish standardized data-sharing agreements across institutions to facilitate multicenter datasets.
Include images from both novice and expert users and multisite data in training data to mitigate domain shift.
Conduct ongoing performance audits of deployed AI models as part of a structured quality assurance process.
Seek FDA agreement on pivotal study design through the presubmission process before starting the study.
Establish baseline performance metrics and monitor change using implementation frameworks after deployment.

screen.reason: This is a framework and commentary paper describing barriers and recommendations for developing, integrating, and adopting point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) AI applications.
